content.title: About
content.content: Winter acorn squash (Acorn squash) is a variety of winter squash with a dark green or gray ribbed skin and a distinctive acorn‑shaped outline. The flesh is pale orange, mildly sweet, and firm. It is sold fresh and uncooked.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Acorn squash belongs to the Cucurbitaceae family, close to zucchini and pumpkin.
In the United States it is called “Acorn squash” because its shape resembles an acorn.
Winter squash can be stored for 3‑4 months in a cool, dry place thanks to its low moisture content.
The seeds are edible and rich in healthy fats; they are often roasted or used in baking.
Acorn squash is high in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.

items.title: Rich in beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene is a precursor of vitamin A, supporting vision and immune function.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: 100 g of raw squash provides about 45 kcal, making it a diet‑friendly food.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts antioxidant protection and enhances iron absorption.

items.title: Minerals: potassium and magnesium
items.content: Potassium helps maintain fluid balance, while magnesium supports muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Squash allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to squash.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Squash contains oxalates, so individuals prone to kidney stones should limit intake.

items.title: Digestive difficulty for young children
items.content: Raw, firm squash can be hard to digest for toddlers; cooking is recommended before serving.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw squash can be sliced thinly and added to salads, used in marinades, or turned into “zoodle” ribbons. It is also commonly roasted, boiled, or stewed, but raw consumption preserves the most vitamins.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the squash in a cool, dry, dark place at 0‑5 °C. For longer storage keep it in the refrigerator in a ventilated bag. Discard any squash that develops soft spots or an off‑odor.
